interactions.label: Which of the following correctly describes the primary complex in childhood tube

params.question: Which of the following correctly describes the primary complex in childhood tuberculosis?

answers.text: Cavitary lesion in the lung apex with contralateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cavitary apical lesions are characteristic of adult reactivation TB. In children, the Ghon focus forms in the mid- or lower lung zones where ventilation is greatest, with ipsilateral — not contralateral — hilar node involvement.

answers.text: Ghon focus in the subpleural parenchyma, ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and connecting lymphangitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The primary complex (Ghon complex) consists of these three elements: the Ghon focus (localised caseous pneumonitis), draining regional lymph node involvement, and the lymphangitis connecting them — the defining lesion of childhood TB.
Miliary nodules represent haematogenous dissemination — a complication that may develop after the primary complex — but they are not part of the primary complex itself.

answers.text: Calcified granuloma in the upper lobe with pleural thickening

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calcified granulomata represent healed, remote primary infection. The primary complex refers to the active initial lesion — Ghon focus, draining nodes, and lymphangitis — not its healed end-state.

overallFeedback.feedback: The primary complex consists of three elements: (1) the Ghon focus — caseous pneumonitis in the mid/lower zones, (2) ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy via lymphatic spread, and (3) connecting lymphangitis. This triad is the defining lesion of childhood TB.

Well done. The primary complex is the pathological cornerstone of paediatric TB — understanding its three components helps you interpret paediatric chest X-rays and anticipate complications from lymph node enlargement.

interactions.label: A 4-year-old household contact of a sputum-positive TB patient receives a Mantou

params.question: A 4-year-old household contact of a sputum-positive TB patient receives a Mantoux test. When reading the result at 48 hours, which measurement determines positivity?

answers.text: Maximum diameter of erythema surrounding the injection site

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Erythema (redness) alone has no diagnostic value in TST interpretation. Only the palpable, raised induration is measured — surrounding erythema is ignored regardless of its size.

answers.text: Total area of skin discolouration calculated in square millimetres

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The TST result is a single linear measurement — the transverse diameter of induration in millimetres — not an area calculation. Skin colour changes alone do not constitute a positive test.

answers.text: Transverse diameter of induration measured perpendicular to the long axis of the forearm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Mantoux test is read by palpating the raised, firm induration and measuring its transverse diameter perpendicular to the forearm's long axis. Erythema without induration is not significant.

answers.text: Longitudinal length of the initial wheal along the forearm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The wheal is the immediate bleb raised during injection — it confirms correct intradermal placement. What is measured at 48–72 hours is the induration, not the original wheal.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct technique: at 48–72 hours, palpate the injection site for the raised, firm induration. Measure its transverse diameter perpendicular to the long axis of the forearm in millimetres. Erythema is ignored.
Excellent. Measuring induration (not erythema), perpendicular to the forearm axis, at 48–72 hours — this three-part rule is the most commonly tested point in Mantoux interpretation.

interactions.label: Why does the diagnosis of childhood tuberculosis require integration of evidence

params.question: Why does the diagnosis of childhood tuberculosis require integration of evidence from multiple domains rather than reliance on a single test?

answers.text: Because a positive Mantoux test alone confirms active disease and is sufficient for treatment initiation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A positive TST indicates prior sensitisation to mycobacterial antigens — it demonstrates TB infection but cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease. Used alone, it would lead to overtreatment.

answers.text: Because childhood TB is paucibacillary and no single test achieves both sufficient sensitivity and specificity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Children harbour low organism loads, making microbiological confirmation difficult. The WHO/IAP therefore recommend combining five evidence domains — epidemiological, clinical, immunological, radiological, and microbiological — for a composite diagnostic decision.

answers.text: Because sputum smear microscopy is the gold standard in children and all other tests serve only to supplement it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sputum smear microscopy has very low sensitivity in children because of the paucibacillary nature of paediatric TB and the difficulty in obtaining quality sputum samples. It is not a reliable stand-alone test in this age group.

answers.text: Because CBNAAT detects all forms of drug-resistant TB with 100% sensitivity, making clinical assessment redundant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CBNAAT has significantly lower sensitivity in paediatric specimens compared to adult sputum, and it detects only rifampicin resistance (via rpoB mutations), not all forms of drug resistance. Clinical assessment remains essential.

overallFeedback.feedback: Childhood TB is paucibacillary — the organism load is low, so cultures and smears are often negative. No single test is both sensitive and specific enough. The WHO/IAP therefore recommend integrating five evidence domains: contact history, symptoms, TST/IGRA, CXR pattern, and specimen results.

Well reasoned. The composite diagnostic approach — epidemiological, clinical, immunological, radiological, and microbiological evidence weighed together — is the most important conceptual shift in paediatric TB compared to adult practice.

interactions.label: A healthy 2-year-old child whose father has been diagnosed with sputum-positive

params.question: A healthy 2-year-old child whose father has been diagnosed with sputum-positive pulmonary TB is asymptomatic with a normal chest X-ray. Which preventive strategy is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Full anti-TB treatment (HRZE) is reserved for confirmed or clinically diagnosed active tuberculosis. An asymptomatic contact with a normal CXR does not have active disease and requires chemoprophylaxis instead.

answers.text: Initiate isoniazid preventive therapy after excluding active tuberculosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. NTEP guidelines recommend isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) for close contacts under 5 years of a sputum-positive case after ruling out active TB. IPT prevents progression from latent infection to active disease.

answers.text: Administer a repeat dose of BCG vaccine to boost immunity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BCG is given as a single dose at birth under India's NIS. Revaccination is not recommended — it does not provide additional protection and cannot prevent acquisition of infection in a close contact.

answers.text: No intervention is needed because BCG vaccination at birth provides lifelong immunity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BCG offers partial protection against severe disseminated forms (miliary TB, TBM) but does not prevent TB infection or confer lifelong immunity. Close contacts of active cases require active evaluation and prophylaxis.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a young, asymptomatic household contact with a normal CXR, the priority is chemoprophylaxis with isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) — not full treatment and not revaccination. BCG does not prevent infection; IPT prevents progression to active disease.

Correct application of preventive strategy. IPT is the key intervention for young household contacts of smear-positive cases — the second level of prevention (chemoprophylaxis) that bridges the gap between BCG's limited protection and the need to treat active disease.
